Capt. John Robert Morrison Jr.

May 14, 1915 – November 18, 2001

An Omaha hangar boy who talked his way into flying lessons in lieu of pay, worked up to instructing — for a flying service, for the University of Omaha, and then for the wartime Navy — and flew for TWA from DC-2s to 707s.

Facts at a glance

Born
May 14, 1915, Omaha, Nebraska
Parents
John Robert Morrison Sr. and Agnes “Lola” (Doolittle) Morrison
School
Abraham Lincoln High School, Council Bluffs — class of 1934
Married
Adele Bernice Jeppesen, June 7, 1939
Work
Flight instructor; TWA pilot, 1940–1975; U.S. Naval Reserve, 1943–1946
Died
November 18, 2001, Miami, Florida
Buried
Cedar Lawn Cemetery, Council Bluffs, Iowa

His story

An Omaha boyhood

John Robert Morrison Jr. was born in Omaha, Nebraska, on May 14, 1915, the son of John Robert Morrison Sr. and Agnes “Lola” (Doolittle) Morrison. He grew up across the river in Council Bluffs and graduated from Abraham Lincoln High School with the class of 1934 — a class year his reunion name tag still carried forty-five years later.

The hangar

His flying life began on the ground. As a boy — possibly still in high school, living with relatives while his father was working in Kansas City for the Union Pacific — he went to work at an Omaha flying service sweeping out the hangar. He was soon allowed to sleep in a loft in the hangar, started helping the mechanics, and, because the service could not pay him much, bargained for flying lessons in lieu of pay. He worked his way up to instructing — which is how he met Adele Jeppesen, one of his student pilots. She went on to earn her pilot’s license, as her son John William states.

The flying service’s name is spelled three ways in the sources, and all three are carried here as given: “Barney Miller Flying Service” in his obituaries, “Burnham-Miller” in his Smithsonian Wall of Honor profile, and “Barnum and Miller” in his son’s written account. No one spelling has been chosen over the others.

Instructor

By the end of the 1930s he was a flight instructor for the University of Omaha’s Civil Aeronautics Authority course. Scrapbook clippings show him teaching Helen Marie Woodson, the only girl in the class of twenty — walking her through a pre-flight line inspection at the tail of the airplane, and fitting her parachute before a lesson on stalls. His CAA instructor qualification at the flying service was recorded in American Aviation on November 15, 1939.

The road to TWA

The next steps are known from the account of his son, John William Morrison, and are labeled as family account. Around 1939, John Jr. and a friend shared a room at the YMCA in St. Paul while he earned an instrument rating at the St. Paul airport. He then took a mechanic’s job at an airline in Kansas City — his son believed it was Capital Airline, while flagging his own doubt about that identification — hoping it would lead to a pilot’s seat. The chief pilot there arranged for him to sit in on Transcontinental & Western Air’s DC-2 ground school across the street; on the last day, T&WA’s chief pilot offered him a job on the spot, and he was checked out in a DC-2 almost immediately.

Shortly before TWA he also worked for Handford Airlines (spelling as printed in his Omaha World-Herald obituary). He was hired by T&WA — later Trans World Airlines — in September 1940, as a DC-2 copilot based in Kansas City.

The Navy years

He was commissioned on March 19, 1943, and entered active service on April 3, 1943, at Corpus Christi, Texas. As a Lieutenant, U.S. Naval Reserve, he served as a Naval Aviator, Flight Instructor, and Check Pilot with VR-3 of the Naval Air Transport Service, at Fairfax and Olathe, Kansas, training and checking the pilots who flew the Navy’s transport routes. On November 29, 1945, he was commended by endorsement (W. M. Collins) for his work. He was separated from the service on March 6, 1946, with a Certificate of Satisfactory Service.

Captain Morrison

After the war he returned to TWA and rose to captain, becoming one of the first captains to transition from the Constellation to the 707. He flew domestic and international routes — family photographs keep him with TWA crews in Cairo and on layovers reaching Lisbon. He retired on May 14, 1975 — his 60th birthday — after 35 years with the airline.

The homes

The family’s homes trace the career: Drake Court, Omaha, after the wedding; then Kansas City and North Kansas City, Missouri; Mission, Kansas; Westfield, New Jersey (from the fall of 1954); Saratoga, California (from about 1961); and finally Miami, Florida (from 1992).

Last years

He was widowed in 1977, when Adele died. In his final years he lived with Parkinson’s. He died on November 18, 2001, at Sun Bay Manor, Miami. His funeral, with military honors, was held on November 23, 2001, and he was buried at Cedar Lawn Cemetery, Council Bluffs, beside Adele. One long-standing confusion can be put to rest plainly: the Social Security Death Index’s “Monterey, California” was a last-residence artifact, not his place of death — his Florida death certificate and both obituaries place his death in Miami.

Timeline

  • 1915May 14 — born in Omaha, Nebraska.
  • 1934Graduates from Abraham Lincoln High School, Council Bluffs.
  • Late 1930sHangar boy at an Omaha flying service — sweeping, sleeping in the loft, helping the mechanics, trading work for flying lessons — and works up to instructing; meets Adele Jeppesen, his student pilot, who went on to earn her pilot’s license.
  • 1939June 7 — marries Adele Jeppesen. November 15 — CAA instructor qualification recorded in American Aviation. About this year, an instrument rating earned in St. Paul (family account).
  • 1940September — hired by Transcontinental & Western Air as a DC-2 copilot, Kansas City, after a brief spell with Handford Airlines.
  • 1943March 19 — commissioned, U.S. Naval Reserve. April 3 — active service begins at Corpus Christi.
  • 1945November 29 — commended by endorsement for his work as a VR-3 flight instructor and check pilot.
  • 1946March 6 — separated from the Navy; returns to TWA.
  • 1954Fall — the family moves to Westfield, New Jersey.
  • c. 1961The family moves to Saratoga, California.
  • 1975May 14 — retires from TWA on his 60th birthday, after 35 years.
  • 1977September 7 — Adele dies; he is widowed.
  • 1992Moves to Miami, Florida.
  • 2001November 18 — dies at Sun Bay Manor, Miami. November 23 — funeral with military honors; buried at Cedar Lawn Cemetery, Council Bluffs.

Sources and open questions

The career and service facts rest on his U.S. Navy Certificate of Satisfactory Service (March 6, 1946), the Naval Air Transport Service commendation endorsement (November 29, 1945), the University of Omaha flying-course clippings, American Aviation (November 15, 1939), his obituaries in the Omaha World-Herald (November 21, 2001) and the Kansas City papers (November 22, 2001), his Florida death certificate, and the documents and photographs of the family archive.

  • The hangar’s name. Spelled “Barney Miller Flying Service” (obituaries), “Burnham-Miller” (Smithsonian Wall of Honor profile), and “Barnum and Miller” (his son’s account). All three are carried as given; the firm’s own records have not been found.
  • The Kansas City mechanic’s job. His son John William believed the airline was Capital Airline but flagged his own doubt — Capital may not have had a Kansas City base. The episode is told here as family account.
  • The Smithsonian profile. His Wall of Honor profile at the National Air and Space Museum is family-supplied and is labeled as such wherever it is used; it is not an independent record.
